slides.title: Money questions you're too shy to ask

slides.q: Can I ask my landlord to lower my rent?
slides.a: You can absolutely ask, and the best time is a month or two before your lease renews. Check what similar places nearby rent for, and remind them you pay on time and take care of the place. Landlords often prefer keeping a good tenant over finding a new one. If they say no, ask for a smaller increase.

slides.q: What happens if I'm late on rent?
slides.a: Usually you'll owe a late fee, which should be spelled out in your lease, and some places limit how much it can be. Being late once rarely leads to eviction, and in most places a landlord can't evict you without going through a legal process. The best move is telling your landlord early and offering a plan to catch up.

slides.q: When do I get my security deposit back?
slides.a: It depends on where you live, but most US states set a deadline, often somewhere between two weeks and a month after you move out. Your landlord can usually keep money for damage beyond normal wear and tear, or for unpaid rent, and many states require an itemized list. Taking photos when you move in and out really helps.

Inflation means prices across the economy rising over time, so the same dollar buys a little less each year. A small, steady amount is normal. That's why a raise smaller than inflation can feel like a pay cut, and why money sitting in a regular savings account slowly loses buying power. It's not just you, groceries really do cost more.

It's a challenge where you stop buying anything that isn't essential for a set time, usually a month. You still pay rent, bills and groceries, but you skip things like takeout, shopping and new subscriptions. It's less about deprivation and more about noticing your habits. Many people come out of it knowing exactly where their money was slipping away.
